I have been working on a touch screen for my printers for a while now, and it has reached the point where I want you to try it. It is called Sailhand, it is open source, and it is a small native app for the display on your Klipper printer.
I started it because I wanted one screen that handles everyday printing and also knows about the multi-material and tool changer setups I run. Sailhand runs on the printer host (a Raspberry Pi, a BTT CB1/CB2 and similar), starts fullscreen at boot and talks to Klipper through Moonraker. It is written in Rust with Slint, so there is no browser and no desktop environment involved. The same app also runs natively on Android, so a phone or tablet works as a printer display as well.
Caution: Sailhand is young software. I tested it on a modified Artillery Sidewinder, on my Voron 2.4 with Happy Hare, and on a friend’s Voron 2.4 with an ERCF, and it runs great there. Tool changers, AFC and Happy Hare with several units are only tested against a simulated printer, not on real machines. Sailhand moves motors, heats and restarts services, so do not leave your printer unattended while you try it. It comes without any warranty, as far as the law allows (see the GPL).
What you can use it for For everyday printing it covers what you would expect from a printer touch screen:
Browse your files with thumbnails, start, pause and cancel a print, exclude objects and pause at a layer. Jog and home the axes, level the bed and run Klipper’s calibration commands. Control heaters, fans and the light, and watch the temperature history. Use the console with your macros, load and unload filament, and handle updates and Wi-Fi. What is cool about it The part I care about most is multi-material and multi-tool support. ERCF, Tradrack, Box Turtle, StealthChanger and more all end up on one Changer page:
Happy Hare 4.1 or newer, also with several units. AFC lanes and the lane in use. Tool changers through klipper-toolchanger. Spoolman: the spool in use, a spool picker with weighing, and a hint before a print when the file and the filament differ. It never blocks a print, it only tells you. A few more things I like:
It shows only what your printer has. No Happy Hare, no Happy Hare page. It also points out things that look unusual, without forbidding them. Native and light. It starts fullscreen at boot via cage, a small Wayland kiosk, and needs no browser. Updates like Mainsail and Fluidd. New versions show up in Moonraker’s update manager. No cloud, no telemetry. Sailhand only talks to your Moonraker. Native Android app. Sailhand also runs as a real native app on Android phones and tablets, not as a web page. Put an old tablet next to the printer and use it as a touch screen, or control the printer from your phone. It talks to the same Moonraker, so you need no extra setup on the printer. Desktop too. You can also run it as a window on a Linux or Windows desktop. Open source. It is licensed under GPL-3.0-or-later, and use is free for everyone. Requirements Klipper with Moonraker, as set up by KIAUH, MainsailOS and similar. A host with Debian 12, Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm or Ubuntu 22.04 (or newer). The installer checks the rest. A display, ideally 5" at 800x480 with touch. Other sizes are scaled. Install Run this on the printer host, as the user that runs Klipper and Moonraker:
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/freakydude/sailhand/releases/latest/download/get-sailhand.sh bash get-sailhand.sh -m http://127.0.0.1:7125 The script picks the build for your system, installs the few packages it needs and sets up a service. Sailhand then starts on the display at every boot.
If you do not want to touch your printer host yet, try the desktop window or the Android app first. The GitHub project describes all the ways to install it.
Try it and tell me On my machines it runs great, but I cannot do much more alone. I only have a few printers to test on, so I need you: install it, play with it and tell me what works and what does not. This is especially true if you run a tool changer, AFC or several Happy Hare units, since I could only test those against a simulated printer.
Report bugs and missing features as GitHub issues. Ask questions or show me your printer on Discord. It is a private project I work on in my spare time, so answers may take a while. A documentation site is coming later.
Conclusion Sailhand is my attempt at a touch screen that fits a printer instead of the other way around. It is ready to try, and I would love to hear how it behaves on your machine. Keep an eye on the printer while you test it, and then let me know what you think.
Further links Sailhand on GitHub Klipper Moonraker Happy Hare AFC klipper-toolchanger Spoolman Slint Please leave a comment if something is wrong or missing, or if you have any questions. Have fun!
If you enjoyed this article and would like to support my work, feel free to buy me a coffee! Your support helps me continue creating content. Thank you!

This is a quick and dirty guide, mostly for my own purposes, on how to flash the BTT Manta M8P CAN and the EBB42 board with Klipper using Katapult. The process should work for other BTT Manta M8P and EBB versions too, but you have to adjust the configuration accordingly.
The BTT Manta M8P CAN board can be flashed and used with Klipper via two different methods: a USB connection or CAN bus. If you are using toolhead boards that support CAN bus, like the EBB36 or EBB42, you have to use CAN bus for the communication between the mainboard and the toolhead board. If you are using toolhead boards that support a USB connection (like the BTT SB2209 USB or the EBB36/42 v2.0), use USB instead.
In general, CAN bus is the preferred method for communication between multiple boards in a 3D printer, as it provides better reliability and performance than USB.
I cover two setups below: my Artillery Sidewinder X2 with CAN bus, and my Voron 2.4 with USB.
Requirements A working Klipper installation on a host system (Raspberry Pi, etc.). Follow the Klipper installation guide if you haven’t done this yet.
Basic knowledge of using the terminal.
dfu-util installed on your host system. You can install it via your package manager. For example, on Debian/Ubuntu-based systems, you can run:
sudo apt-get install dfu-util python3-serial A USB cable to connect the BTT Manta M8P board to your host system for flashing Katapult and Klipper.
A CAN bus connection between the BTT Manta M8P board and the BTT EBB42 board for communication (CAN setup only).
Configure CAN bus on the host system There are many ways to set up CAN bus on your host system. I recommend using systemd-networkd for this. Here is a quick example.
Add the following file /etc/systemd/network/80-can.link:
[Match] Type=can [Link] TransmitQueueLength=128 Then add the following file /etc/systemd/network/80-can.network:
[Match] Name=can0 [CAN] BitRate=1000000 Run the following commands to load this configuration:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart systemd-networkd Artillery Sidewinder X2 setup (CAN bus) I replaced the original Artillery mainboard with a BTT Manta M8P v1.1 running in CAN mode. I replaced the original Artillery toolhead board with a BTT EBB42 v1.2 running in CAN mode. Flash the BTT Manta M8P v1.1 in CAN mode Flash Katapult to the Manta M8P This step is only necessary if you have a brand new BTT Manta M8P board without Katapult installed. If Katapult is already installed, you can skip this step.
Download Katapult.
cd ~ git clone https://github.com/Arksine/katapult cd katapult Configure Katapult for the BTT Manta M8P v1.1 CAN:
make menuconfig Be aware that I have also enabled the PC3 GPIO pin. If you have connected a device like the BTT Relay V1.2 to the PS-ON GPIO pin, the power supply is switched via this pin.
Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the firmware-bootloader package:
make -j Flash Katapult:
sudo dfu-util -R -a 0 -s 0x08000000:mass-erase:force -D ~/katapult/out/katapult.bin Reset the board (or power it off and on). Katapult should now be installed, and the status LED will blink.
Flash Klipper to the Manta M8P Configure the Klipper firmware for the BTT Manta M8P v1.1 CAN:
cd ~ cd klipper make menuconfig Be aware that I have also enabled the PC3 GPIO pin. If you have connected a device like the BTT Relay V1.2 to the PS-ON GPIO pin, the power supply is switched via this pin.
Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the Klipper firmware:
make -j Stop the Klipper service first:
sudo service klipper stop Flash Klipper.
Depending on whether Klipper is already running on the board (update workflow), you need to switch into bootloader mode first. Run the following command to do so:
~/klippy-env/bin/python ~/katapult/scripts/flashtool.py -i can0 -u <CANBUS-UUID> -r Replace <CANBUS-UUID> with the actual CAN bus UUID of your board (configured in printer.cfg in the [mcu] section as canbus_uuid).
Now you should get something similar to this:
Canbus Bridge detected at /sys/bus/usb/devices/1-1.4 Connecting to CAN UUID 4a0cb5640a86 on interface can0 Sending bootloader jump command... Waiting for USB Reconnect...done Detected new USB Device: 1d50:6177 katapult stm32g0b1xx Katapult detected at serial port /dev/ttyACM0 Bootloader Request Complete Your board is now in bootloader mode. You can connect to it via the serial port /dev/ttyACM0.
Finally, flash the Klipper firmware:
cd ~/klipper make flash FLASH_DEVICE=/dev/ttyACM0 This should finish with a CAN Flash Success message.
Restart Klipper to apply the changes:
sudo service klipper restart Flash the BTT EBB42 v1.2 in CAN mode Flash Katapult to the EBB42 This step is only necessary if you have a brand new BTT EBB42 board without Katapult installed. If Katapult is already installed, you can skip this step.
Connect your EBB42 via USB and prepare it for flashing Katapult.
Power off your printer. Unplug the CAN bus cable from the EBB42 board to avoid any power issues. Temporarily bridge the 5V jumper on the EBB42 board to power it via USB. Put the board into DFU mode by holding the BOOT button while plugging in the USB cable. Alternatively, press and hold the BOOT button, press reset, release reset, and then release BOOT. The board should now be in DFU mode and ready to be flashed. If needed, download Katapult.
cd ~ git clone https://github.com/Arksine/katapult cd katapult Configure Katapult for the BTT EBB42 v1.2 CAN:
cd ~/katapult make menuconfig Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the firmware-bootloader package:
make -j Flash Katapult:
sudo dfu-util -R -a 0 -s 0x08000000:mass-erase:force -D ~/katapult/out/katapult.bin This should finish with a File downloaded successfully message.
Remove the 5V jumper, unplug your USB cable, and power off your printer. Connect your CAN bus cable to the EBB42 board, then power on. Katapult should now be installed.
Flash Klipper to the EBB42 Configure the Klipper firmware for the BTT EBB42 v1.2 CAN:
cd ~ cd klipper make menuconfig Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the Klipper firmware:
make -j Stop the Klipper service first:
sudo service klipper stop Query the CAN bus UUID of the EBB42 board:
~/klippy-env/bin/python ~/klipper/scripts/canbus_query.py can0 You should get something like this: Found canbus_uuid=c239709a91c7, Application: CanBoot
Make a note of the canbus_uuid. It should be the UUID of your EBB42 board, and you need it for the next step.
Flash Klipper to the EBB42:
~/klippy-env/bin/python3 ~/katapult/scripts/flash_can.py -i can0 -f ~/klipper/out/klipper.bin -u <CANBUS-UUID> Replace <CANBUS-UUID> with the actual CAN bus UUID of your board (noted from the last step, or configured in printer.cfg in the [mcu ebb42] section as canbus_uuid).
This should result in something like this:
Verifying canbus connection Flashing '/home/freaky/klipper/out/klipper.bin'... [##################################################] Write complete: 21 pages Verifying (block count = 649)... [##################################################] Verification Complete: SHA = 0CD35886C377A91B5AB0E0AD44684CB24DEBE05E Programming Complete If you get any errors and you have double-checked your CAN bus UUID, try to reset the EBB42 board by power cycling your printer, and try again. If this does not work, start over with flashing Katapult to the EBB42 board.
Restart Klipper to apply the changes:
sudo service klipper restart Voron 2.4 setup (USB) Mainboard: BTT Manta M8P v2.0 (USB mode) Toolhead board: BTT EBB SB2209 v1.10 USB Flash the BTT EBB SB2209 USB Configure the Klipper firmware for the BTT EBB SB2209 USB:
cd ~ cd klipper make menuconfig Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the Klipper firmware:
make -j Stop the Klipper service first:
sudo service klipper stop Flash Klipper:
cd ~/klipper make flash FLASH_DEVICE=2e8a:0003 This should result in something like this:
Flashing out/klipper.uf2 to 2e8a:0003 sudo lib/rp2040_flash/rp2040_flash out/klipper.uf2 Loaded UF2 image with 166 pages Found rp2040 device on USB bus 1 address 9 Flashing... Resetting interface Locking Exiting XIP mode Erasing Flashing Rebooting device Restart Klipper to apply the changes:
sudo service klipper restart Flash the BTT Manta M8P v2.0 in USB mode Configure the Klipper firmware for the BTT Manta M8P v2.0 USB:
cd ~ cd klipper make menuconfig Be aware that I have also enabled the PD14 GPIO pin. If you have connected a device like the BTT Relay V1.2 to the PS-ON GPIO pin, the power supply is switched via this pin.
Save and exit with Quit and Yes.
Build the Klipper firmware:
make -j Stop the Klipper service first:
sudo service klipper stop Flash Klipper.
If you are doing this for the first time, you need to put the board into bootloader mode first. To do so, hold the BOOT button while plugging in the USB cable. Alternatively, press and hold the BOOT button, press reset, release reset, and then release BOOT.
After that, you can flash the firmware:
sudo dfu-util -R -a 0 -s 0x08000000:mass-erase:force -D ~/klipper/out/klipper.bin If this results in an error, you probably already have Klipper running on the board.
In this case, you can use the following command to flash the firmware. The xxxxxxxxxxx part of the path may differ in your case, so adjust it accordingly.
Determine the correct serial path by listing the devices:
ls /dev/serial/by-id/usb-Klipper_stm32h723xx_* cd ~/klipper make flash FLASH_DEVICE=/dev/serial/by-id/usb-Klipper_stm32h723xx_xxxxxxxxxxx-if00 This results in something like this:
Downloading element to address = 0x08000000, size = 41508 Erase [=========================] 100% 41508 bytes Erase done. Download [=========================] 100% 41508 bytes Download done. File downloaded successfully ... Ignore the errors below it, you should be good to go.
Restart Klipper to apply the changes:
sudo service klipper restart Conclusion After these steps, your mainboard and toolhead board run current Klipper firmware, either over CAN bus with Katapult as the bootloader (Sidewinder X2) or over USB (Voron 2.4).
Further links Klipper documentation Klipper on GitHub Katapult on GitHub Dr. Klipper wiki: BTT Manta (CAN bridge) Dr. Klipper wiki: BTT EBB42 (CAN) Please leave a comment if something is wrong or missing, or if you have any questions. Have fun!

One of the most common frustrations among 3D printing enthusiasts is the inaccuracy of the print time estimates provided by slicers and firmware. This can lead to unexpected delays and scheduling issues.
Fortunately, with Klipper you can significantly improve the accuracy of these estimates by using the Klipper Estimator plugin, together with the proper configuration in Moonraker, Mainsail, and KlipperScreen.
Configure Klipper Estimator in Moonraker First, enable the Klipper Estimator plugin in Moonraker. This plugin analyzes your G-code files and provides more accurate print time estimates based on factors such as print speed and acceleration.
To enable the plugin, add the following section to your moonraker.conf file:
[analysis] auto_dump_default_config: true enable_auto_analysis: true enable_estimator_updates: true Next, configure Mainsail to use the slicer estimates where possible. Go to Mainsail > Settings:
Print progress calculation → “Slicer (M73)” ETA calculation method → “Slicer” Estimate time calculation → “File, Filament” Set up KlipperScreen to show the estimated time. Open KlipperScreen.conf and add the following to the main section:
[main] print_estimate_method = slicer Or use the UI to set it.
Restart Moonraker and KlipperScreen to apply the changes.
What Klipper Estimator takes into account The Klipper Estimator plugin provides more accurate print time predictions by analyzing your G-code and considering several important factors, including:
Configured maximum speeds and accelerations: It uses your printer’s actual speed and acceleration limits set in printer.cfg, rather than generic slicer assumptions. Movement planning: It simulates how Klipper will execute each move, including acceleration and deceleration phases, to estimate realistic timings. Extruder and toolhead changes: The estimator accounts for tool changes, retractions, and priming moves, which can add up over long prints. Layer changes and Z-moves: Vertical movements and layer transitions are included in the calculation. Pauses and delays: Any G-code commands that introduce pauses or dwell times are factored into the estimate. Firmware retraction and pressure advance: If you use features like pressure advance or firmware retraction, the estimator includes their impact on print timing. By considering these real-world printer behaviors, Klipper Estimator can provide a much more reliable print time estimate than slicers alone.
Conclusion With these simple steps, you can significantly improve the print time estimates in Klipper. The Klipper Estimator plugin takes your printer’s speed and acceleration settings into account to provide a more accurate estimate. This will help you plan your printing schedule better and reduce the frustration caused by inaccurate estimates.
Happy printing!

enable_auto_analysis: true

  3. Set up KlipperScreen to show the estimated time. Open KlipperScreen.conf and add the following to the main section:

    [main]
print_estimate_method = slicer

    Or use the UI to set it.

  4. Restart Moonraker and KlipperScreen to apply the changes.

This step-by-step guide explains how to flash Armbian Linux onto the BigTreeTech CB1 eMMC compute module. I describe the process for a Windows machine, but the steps are very similar for Linux users.
The eMMC version of the CB1 has built-in storage, which makes the process slightly more complicated than flashing an SD card for the non-eMMC versions.
Requirements You will need the following items to complete the process.
Hardware A BigTreeTech RPI adapter or a BigTreeTech Manta board to provide the necessary USB and LAN connectors. A USB-C cable to connect and power the CB1 from your Windows machine. For added reliability, I recommend putting a USB hub with a dedicated power adapter in between. Software A universal USB driver. See Zadig. Allwinner tools to switch the CB1 into USB device mode. See sunxi-tools or the sunxi wiki. An Armbian Linux image of your choice. See Armbian for CB1. An image flashing tool. I used Balena Etcher. Switch the CB1 into eMMC USB storage mode Set the DIP switches (USB OTG) and (RPI BOOT) to ON to enter BOOT mode.
Install the universal USB driver Connect your CB1 to your Windows machine. Install and start Zadig. Download and run Zadig. List all USB devices. In Zadig, list all USB devices on your machine. Identify your CB1. Look for your device, which will likely appear as an unknown device. Try each device until you find the one with the correct USB ID. If you cannot find it, make sure that the DIP switches are set correctly and that your USB connection is working properly. Install the driver. Enable the CB1 eMMC as a USB storage device Download the required files.
Obtain sunxi-fel.exe and u-boot-sunxi-cb1-emmc.bin from sunxi-tools. Open a Windows Command Prompt.
Press <WIN>+<R>, type cmd, and press <ENTER>. Run the sunxi-fel command.
Navigate to the folder containing the downloaded sunxi-tools and run the following command: sunxi-fel.exe uboot u-boot-sunxi-cb1-emmc.bin This will switch the CB1 into USB storage mode. Flash the Armbian image Start Balena Etcher. Select the downloaded Armbian image and flash your CB1 (it should appear as a storage device). There is no need to change the default settings. Begin the flashing process. Apply the mandatory Armbian configuration Modify the armbianEnv.txt file.
Replace the line
fdtfile=allwinner/sun50i-h616-bigtreetech-cb1-sd.dtb with
fdtfile=allwinner/sun50i-h616-bigtreetech-cb1-emmc.dtb This change activates the eMMC storage as the boot device. You can revert to the previous setting to boot from an SD card if needed.
Clean up Unmount the eMMC. Safely eject the eMMC storage from your system. Disconnect the power. Remove the USB cable or power source. Reset the DIP switches. Set the DIP switches (USB OTG) and (RPI BOOT) back to OFF to exit BOOT mode. Conclusion Congratulations! You should now have successfully flashed Armbian onto your BigTreeTech CB1. You can connect the CB1 to a display and keyboard, or to your network, and follow the official Armbian documentation for further setup.

If you have been following my recent posts, you know that I switched from Marlin to Klipper on my Artillery Sidewinder X2. If you have done the same, you may be experiencing the same problem as I did. You have already asked me how much better the printing results are with Klipper, but that is another topic.
Our integrated display is useless!
But I found a solution. It is not perfect yet, but more than OK for my main use cases. After reading a lot of discussions, I understood the relationships between the printer mainboard, the included TFT, Marlin, and Klipper, and I got an idea.
So I started an experiment, which I think was successful. It resulted in an open source project, which is an experiment in itself.
So what am I talking about? I made the integrated display (and potentially any supported BigTreeTech TFT) work with Klipper.
Update (November 2026): The BigTreeTech issue about the GD32F305 TFT is closed now, and the project has an additional macro file for a status LED. But the official firmware release Vx.x.28 is reported not to flash on the Sidewinder X2 screen, so check the requirements section.
Caution: As always with my other posts and projects, I am not a company. I do this in my spare time, mostly because I am really excited to make these things work and to improve them. I tested all of this only with my own printer and the setup around it. I did my best to make it all work without problems. However, there is no warranty. Be careful, watch your printer, and double-check things. Use it as it is. I assume no liability for damages or consequences of any kind.
Requirements A Raspberry Pi or BigTreeTech CB1 (most of you already use one for Klipper) A level shifter (a cheap part, for example) A BigTreeTech TFT in touch mode (I used the BTT TFT28 with the GD32F305 chipset in my Artillery Sidewinder X2) Most things should work with the official Artillery firmware. To get all the features, flash the open source TouchScreenFirmware. Support for the GD32F305 TFT controller was requested in this issue, which was closed as completed in February 2024. The repository contains the Artillery TFT28 V3.0.5 (GD32F305) bootloader, but a user reports that the release Vx.x.28 does not flash on a Sidewinder X2 with a GD32F305 TFT28 (modified versions work). I could not verify the current state myself, so check that issue before you flash. Thanks for all the work, guys! So, let’s start hacking and improving your printer.
Wire the display First, you need to wire things up. Disconnect the display from your mainboard. It needs to be connected to your Raspberry Pi instead.
I made a little schematic that shows how to connect your Pi through a level shifter to the UART (serial) interface of your BTT TFT (or a compatible one, like the one in the Artillery Sidewinder X2). It is really important to use a level shifter here. If the UART pins of your Raspberry Pi GPIO get 5V, they will be irreparably damaged and burn. Be careful!
That is not a mistake: make sure that somewhere between the display UART and the Raspberry Pi UART you have a TX (transmit) and RX (receive) crossover. It allows a bidirectional connection between them.
That is all the hardware magic you need.
Set up the software The hardware wiring is only part of the story. The following schematic shows the relevant components, their connections, and the type of data transferred. I hope it helps you understand the concept.
You can find my project at https://github.com/freakydude/klipper-serial-btt.
Set up the serial software bridge with a systemd service Prepare your Raspberry Pi or BigTreeTech CB1 (or similar) as described in the project readme.
Set up Klipper (with Mainsail) As you can see in the schematic above, your touchscreen and the BigTreeTech firmware running on it are based on G-code. Basically, it sends and receives Marlin-compatible G-code upon interaction. Therefore, for Klipper to communicate with the display in a useful way, we need to provide the necessary G-code macros for Klipper.
Prepare your Klipper and Mainsail configs as described in the project readme.
To keep the overview, I have split the macros into several files: the example file below, and four files in the fd-macros folder of the project.
fd-macros-example.cfg For full Mainsail feature support, you must add some macros. Mainsail even has a self-updating repository of what you can add to your Klipper and Mainsail configuration. To enable some functions on your TFT, some of these macros need to be changed. But due to technical limitations, I don’t know a way to override G-code commands twice (which is what we would have to do).
This has consequences:
At the moment I don’t know a way to extend or replace their macros, but I need to. So I reimplemented the needed functionality. This makes me kind of sad. It also means you can’t use their config files, because they conflict with my scripts. I made this file, and if you look at it, it mostly just calls “internal” macros starting with _FD_. This way I’m trying to give you the ability to “override” my individual scripts with whatever you want, and hopefully not get into conflicts. So if you have an Artillery Sidewinder X2 and just want to get started, use this file as it is and feel freakyDude’s printing style ;-).
If you need or want to have your own scripts, don’t include this file. Instead, copy it completely, include your copy, still call the internal macros, and adapt it to your needs. It is kind of a front for the other macros.
fd-macros/klipper-modules.cfg This file activates all the modules needed to support all the features required by both Mainsail and the BTT touchscreen. If you have already configured some of the modules, you can delete them from your other config files.
fd-macros/mainsail-support.cfg This file contains all the “internal” macros to support the current Mainsail features required by both Mainsail and the BTT touchscreen. I would not suggest replacing them. Use them as they are.
If there are problems with it, let’s discuss the issue and create a pull request.
fd-macros/bigtreetech-support.cfg Similar to mainsail-support.cfg, this file contains all the “internal” macros to support the current BTT touchscreen features. Mostly, this is a subset of the Marlin G-codes. It also sends some information to the display, so it communicates in both directions. I only implemented what I needed and tested the features, and some things don’t fit between Klipper and Marlin. I think it is a good start.
As with the file above, use the macros as they are. If there are problems with them, let’s discuss the issue and create a pull request.
fd-macros/status-led-support.cfg This file visualizes some printer states with a Neopixel or Dotstar LED, for example the extruder LED of the Sidewinder X2. It is optional, and it is ignored unless your printer.cfg has a [neopixel statusled] or [dotstar statusled] section. The project readme has an example section for the Sidewinder X2.
Set up your slicer To enable the progress and color change features, configure your slicer as described in the project readme.
Conclusion If you have successfully followed my instructions, you may be one of the first people on the planet to have this combination: a BTT touchscreen in Marlin touch mode, working on a printer driven by Klipper. And yes, since we are all green these days, you did not throw away your working hardware. Congratulations!
For further steps and more details, it is always a good idea to go through the very good official documentation.

Input shaping (also called resonance compensation) is a technique to reduce vibrations and resonances by proactively adjusting the printer movements. It increases the maximum possible printer speed without reducing the print quality. You can find more details in the Klipper Resonance Compensation documentation.
This article focuses on the Klipper firmware, but Marlin has also had a simpler input shaping since version 2.1.2 (see M593). It supports only the ZV shaper, and Marlin does not provide accelerometer-based tuning: you tune it with a ringing tower or a frequency sweep.
There is also a manual way to determine the resonance frequencies. This post shows you the steps to measure the frequencies with an ADXL345 accelerometer chip instead. You can get one for a few bucks.
Ready? Let’s start!
Update (November 2026): The software installation command now follows the current Klipper documentation (libopenblas-dev, numpy<1.26), and the Marlin remark is corrected: Marlin has simple ZV input shaping since version 2.1.2. The SHAPER_CALIBRATE commands are split per axis, and the diagrams of the manual measurement are embedded.
Requirements Your printer (tested with the Artillery Sidewinder X2) A working Klipper installation (tested with MainsailOS) Jumper cables or similar ADXL345 accelerometer module An adapter to mount it on your extruder (see my design on Thingiverse) Raspberry Pi (or any other connected MCU with an SPI interface) Install and wire the accelerometer As always, Klipper has very clean and useful documentation. It describes well how to wire the accelerometer.
Here is an example of how to connect your ADXL345 to the SPI interface of the Raspberry Pi. It is a copy of the relevant wiring diagram:
I used standard jumper cables for that task, but if you want to do some crafting, go ahead.
If you have a Sidewinder X1/X2 or Genius Pro, you can use my mount from Thingiverse to install the accelerometer on your extruder. I suggest V2: the sensor is parallel to the xy-plane and mounted with screws. Because those printers are bed slingers, the measurement of the resonance frequency should be split. To measure the frequency of the y-axis, you should install the accelerometer on your heated bed. I made an adapter for that too. (Thanks to Paradisebaker for clarifying that.)
If you own another printer, you have to look for a different mounting solution.
Build a Klipper MCU for the Pi To make use of the SPI interface, you need to build and set up an additional Klipper firmware for your target. Then you can configure it as an MCU in your config files.
Install the software Detailed Klipper documentation
Log in to your MainsailOS Pi.
Make sure the needed packages are installed. (In newer MainsailOS versions, everything is already installed.)
sudo apt update sudo apt install python3-numpy python3-matplotlib libatlas-base-dev libopenblas-dev ~/klippy-env/bin/pip install -v "numpy<1.26" Build the secondary MCU for the Pi RPi Micro-Controller documentation
First, make sure the Linux SPI driver is enabled by running sudo raspi-config and enabling SPI under the “Interfacing options” menu.
Next, compile the Klipper micro-controller code, start by configuring it for the “Linux process”:
cd ~/klipper/ make menuconfig In the menu, set “Microcontroller Architecture” to “Linux process,” then save and exit.
Build and install the new micro-controller code, run:
sudo service klipper stop make flash sudo service klipper start Copy the matching klipper-mcu service, then enable and start it.
cd ~/klipper/ sudo cp ./scripts/klipper-mcu.service /etc/systemd/system/ sudo systemctl enable --now klipper-mcu.service Configure the newly compiled RPi MCU in your printer.cfg
[mcu rpi] serial: /tmp/klipper_host_mcu [adxl345] cs_pin: rpi:None axes_map: -y, x, z # Depends on mounting direction. Works for my V2 Mount [resonance_tester] accel_chip: adxl345 probe_points: 150, 150, 20 # mid of your bed (Sidewinder size: 300x300mm) Test the accelerometer Open your G-code console (for example in Mainsail).
Check if the accelerometer responds. If not, double-check the steps above and the Klipper documentation.
ACCELEROMETER_QUERY The output should look similar to this:
accelerometer values (x, y, z): 536.266849, -888.247130, 9918.759623 Check that the sensor and wires don’t have too much noise:
MEASURE_AXES_NOISE All values should be below 100:
Axes noise for xy-axis accelerometer: 11.789601 (x), 16.017559 (y), 29.190110 (z) If you have problems, see Checking the setup
Measure resonances manually Test the x-axis resonances in the G-code console (for example in Mainsail). Mount your ADXL345 on your extruder.
TEST_RESONANCES AXIS=X Log in to your Raspberry Pi terminal (with SSH).
Run calibrate_shaper.py with the generated CSV file. This also generates a nice diagram of the measured and calculated frequencies.
Example:
~/klipper/scripts/calibrate_shaper.py /tmp/resonances_x_*.csv -o ~/printer_data/config/shaper_calibrate_x.png Fitted shaper 'zv' frequency = 53.8 Hz (vibrations = 11.0%, smoothing ~= 0.060) To avoid too much smoothing with 'zv', suggested max_accel <= 11300 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper 'mzv' frequency = 55.0 Hz (vibrations = 0.0%, smoothing ~= 0.067) To avoid too much smoothing with 'mzv', suggested max_accel <= 8900 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper 'ei' frequency = 69.4 Hz (vibrations = 1.4%, smoothing ~= 0.067) To avoid too much smoothing with 'ei', suggested max_accel <= 9000 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper '2hump_ei' frequency = 81.8 Hz (vibrations = 0.0%, smoothing ~= 0.081) To avoid too much smoothing with '2hump_ei', suggested max_accel <= 7400 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper '3hump_ei' frequency = 98.4 Hz (vibrations = 0.0%, smoothing ~= 0.085) To avoid too much smoothing with '3hump_ei', suggested max_accel <= 7100 mm/sec^2 Recommended shaper is mzv @ 55.0 Hz The diagram is from another measurement run than the output above, so the values differ a bit.
Test the y-axis resonances in the G-code console (for example in Mainsail). Mount your ADXL345 on your heated bed. There is also an adapter on my Thingiverse page.
TEST_RESONANCES AXIS=Y Log in to your Raspberry Pi terminal (with SSH).
Run calibrate_shaper.py with the generated CSV file. This also generates a nice diagram of the measured and calculated frequencies.
Example:
~/klipper/scripts/calibrate_shaper.py /tmp/resonances_y_*.csv -o ~/printer_data/config/shaper_calibrate_y.png Fitted shaper 'zv' frequency = 39.6 Hz (vibrations = 18.1%, smoothing ~= 0.102) To avoid too much smoothing with 'zv', suggested max_accel <= 6100 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper 'mzv' frequency = 30.8 Hz (vibrations = 1.0%, smoothing ~= 0.215) To avoid too much smoothing with 'mzv', suggested max_accel <= 2800 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper 'ei' frequency = 41.6 Hz (vibrations = 1.3%, smoothing ~= 0.186) To avoid too much smoothing with 'ei', suggested max_accel <= 3200 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper '2hump_ei' frequency = 40.2 Hz (vibrations = 0.0%, smoothing ~= 0.334) To avoid too much smoothing with '2hump_ei', suggested max_accel <= 1700 mm/sec^2 Fitted shaper '3hump_ei' frequency = 48.0 Hz (vibrations = 0.5%, smoothing ~= 0.356) To avoid too much smoothing with '3hump_ei', suggested max_accel <= 1500 mm/sec^2 Recommended shaper is ei @ 41.6 Hz Again, this diagram is from another measurement run than the output above.
Configure the input_shaper section in printer.cfg. You can take the following snippet and replace the frequencies and algorithm with your calculated and chosen ones.
Example:
[input_shaper] shaper_freq_x: 55.0 shaper_type_x: mzv shaper_freq_y: 41.6 shaper_type_y: ei Calibrate automatically (alternative) If you are not interested in the details, you can use the automatic SHAPER_CALIBRATE script. See the Input Shaper auto-calibration documentation.
In short:
SHAPER_CALIBRATE or, if you have to move the accelerometer between the axes as on a bed slinger, one axis at a time:
SHAPER_CALIBRATE AXIS=X SHAPER_CALIBRATE AXIS=Y Don’t forget to save your config:
SAVE_CONFIG Conclusion I hope this was straightforward and you could successfully measure your resonances. Now you should be able to print faster with your Artillery Sidewinder X2. Try to increase your acceleration and speed.
Further links For further steps and more details, it is always a very good idea to walk through the official documentation:
Klipper documentation Mainsail documentation Please leave a comment if something is wrong or missing, or if you have any questions. Have fun!

The stock filament runout sensor is connected to the TFT display controller board. This is the reason why neither the Marlin firmware nor Klipper recognizes it by default. For both firmwares, you have to connect the sensor to the Artillery Ruby mainboard instead of the TFT controller board.
In short:
Connect your filament runout sensor to the z-endstop pins. Configure a Klipper filament switch sensor section with the z-endstop pin (PA0). The long version has a few minor problems to solve:
Different voltage (3.3V vs. 5V) Connecting the wires to free pins Configuring Klipper Caution: Do this only if you feel experienced enough. You do it at your own risk, and you will probably lose the Artillery warranty. I am not responsible for damages of any kind.
Check the voltage The pins of the Artillery Ruby mainboard have either 5V or 24V. But the filament runout sensor is connected to the TFT controller at a 3.3V pin.
Sadly, no specs about the runout sensor are in circulation, so nobody knows if 5V would be too much for it. But after some investigation, I found that all similar sensors have a voltage range of 3~5V. So I tried it, and it worked. Of course, it’s your own decision and risk.
Connect the wires I see two possibilities for connecting the filament runout sensor wires to the correct pins. The fast version works without opening the printer case. A beautiful solution, on the other hand, requires opening the printer case.
The fast and dirty option Build yourself an adapter from a male JST-XH 2.54mm connector with three pins to your z-endstop JST SM connector with three pins. The z-endstop plug is fixed on the right side with adhesive tape.
You need these two connector types:
JST XH 2.54 connector JST SM connector Or you can just use some jumper cables. These are the pins of the filament runout sensor: If the state LED of your filament runout sensor is lit, your connection should be fine.
The beautiful option The more beautiful option is to do nothing on the outside of your Sidewinder X2. Instead, open your printer case at the bottom. (As with any other modification, know what you are doing and be aware that your warranty will be lost.)
The original cable comes from the small z-axis board and goes to the TFT controller board. Unplug it from the TFT controller board and plug it into the z-endstop connector of your Artillery Ruby board. Fix it with hot glue.
There is still one problem. In my case, the original cable was not long enough, so I had to extend it. I did that with the adapter cable from the fast and dirty option above. It would be better to replace the original cable with one that is long enough.
Finally, it’s time to configure Klipper.
Configure Klipper At the end, you have to configure Klipper to use the newly connected filament runout sensor. That’s probably the easiest part.
Open your printer.cfg and add the following section
[filament_switch_sensor filament] pause_on_runout: True # Starts the PAUSE g-code script if filament runs out runout_gcode: M117 Filament runout # Optional insert_gcode: M117 Filament insert # Optional switch_pin: PA0 # the z-endstop pin and restart the Klipper firmware afterwards.
If you did it right, you will see a new entry in the Miscellaneous section of your Mainsail web UI. It toggles when you insert or remove filament in your filament runout sensor. Also, the status LED switches between red and green as before.
Conclusion By following this post, you not only re-enabled your filament runout sensor, you also enabled it for real for the first time. Even if you are still using the Marlin firmware, you now have the possibility to configure it in your firmware. I still don’t know why Artillery didn’t just connect it right out of the box. But now it works, and maybe you had some fun fixing the sensor.
Please leave a comment if something is wrong or missing, or if you have any questions. Have fun!

Klipper lets you add G-code macros or even overwrite existing G-codes. By default, Klipper only knows the standard G-codes (described in the Klipper documentation). You have to configure everything that goes beyond that. Typical scenarios are filament runout, pause and resume print, filament change, and cancel objects. For the Artillery Sidewinder X2, you can also add some macros that define what the Neopixel LED on your extruder should do.
The basic idea is often not mine. Instead, I gathered examples from the documentation and adapted them to the Sidewinder X2 and my needs. My advice is that you start the same way. But you can also just copy mine for your first steps with your Sidewinder.
Update (November 2026): The Sidewinder X2 printer.cfg is part of the official Klipper examples, the ADXL345 post exists, and the bundled mainsail.cfg is the 2022 state. Today MainsailOS ships mainsail.cfg itself, and you customize it with a _CLIENT_VARIABLE macro.
Set up Mainsail and Klipper For the basic setup of Klipper with Mainsail, you should start by configuring your machine. Set up the printer and Mainsail, and add some basic must-have macros.
Log in to the Mainsail web page on your Raspberry Pi, or wherever you run it. Navigate to the config files. I suggest splitting your configuration into files according to their content. First add or edit the following three config files. The printer.cfg contains all configuration of your Sidewinder X2 printer hardware. It also includes a reference to the next two config files. The macros.cfg contains basic G-code macros to start, end, pause, resume, and cancel the print. In my case, there are also some helper scripts, for example to enable the extruder LED. And lastly the mainsail.cfg (the 2022 state, see below). It configures the basic features in combination with the Mainsail UI, for example to enable the virtual SD card, exclude objects, or pause and resume prints. The printer.cfg file The printer.cfg file represents the printer hardware. In this case, it is the stock Artillery Sidewinder X2, sold in 2022. I already introduced the printer.cfg in my last blog post. I created a pull request to the official Klipper repository, and it was merged on October 22, 2022. You find the basic printer.cfg example for the Artillery Sidewinder X2 in the Klipper config examples.
In another post, I show you how to add ADXL345 support to enable automatic and precise calibration of the resonance compensation: Install the ADXL345 and Calibrate Input Shaping.
See more about the configuration of your hardware in the excellent Klipper configuration reference.
Don’t forget to calibrate at least your z_offset carefully before printing. If you don’t, you could damage your heated bed. See bed leveling for more instructions.
The mainsail.cfg file The mainsail.cfg file represents the minimum configuration for Mainsail. At the time of writing in 2022, I built it from the Mainsail documentation and shipped it as a local file next to the printer.cfg. It is the 2022 state, so please treat it as a historical example.
Today, MainsailOS already provides a mainsail.cfg from the mainsail-config repository. It bundles everything Mainsail requires: [virtual_sdcard], [display_status], [pause_resume], and the PAUSE, RESUME, and CANCEL_PRINT macros. You only add [include mainsail.cfg] to your printer.cfg, as my printer.cfg above does, and you don’t edit that file. To change its behavior (park position, retraction, and so on), copy the _CLIENT_VARIABLE macro into your printer.cfg and override only the variables you need. The Mainsail documentation of mainsail.cfg lists all variables.
If you use the current mainsail.cfg, you don’t need my local copy, and my PAUSE, RESUME, and CANCEL_PRINT macros in macros.cfg may duplicate its macros. In my 2022 setup, I moved the G-code macros to an additional macros.cfg file, and my local mainsail.cfg also enables [exclude_object] and [gcode_arcs], which the Mainsail documentation does not list for the current file.
The macros.cfg file The macros.cfg file contains all our basic G-code macros. That includes the START_PRINT, END_PRINT, PRIME_LINE, PRESENT_PRINT, PAUSE, RESUME, and CANCEL_PRINT macros. In addition, I added some very basic macros to enable, set, and disable the LED under the extruder (ELED_ON, SET_ELED, and ELED_OFF).
Check the result If you did everything right, Mainsail shows no errors or warnings on its dashboard. Mainsail is ready to print.
But before printing, make sure you read the next section.
Set up the slicer (Cura) I will show you how to set up your Sidewinder X2 using the example of the UltiMaker Cura slicer, especially the start and end G-code. Of course, you can adapt this to the other great slicers out there.
If you used Marlin before, you don’t have to change the printer and printhead settings. If not, the easiest way for an initial configuration is to add an Artillery Sidewinder X1 as your printer and rename it to X2. It has the same settings.
What’s new with Klipper? As you can configure your own G-code macros in Klipper, it’s good practice to replace the default Cura start and end G-code scripts with your own G-code macros. If you use my macros.cfg above, all the start and end logic is defined there.
Just call the START_PRINT and END_PRINT G-code macros in the Start G-code and End G-code sections of your Cura machine settings, as seen in the screenshot above.
For copy and paste:
Start G-code START_PRINT BED_TEMP={material_bed_temperature_layer_0} EXTRUDER_TEMP={material_print_temperature_layer_0} It calls the START_PRINT macro from macros.cfg with the material print temperatures configured in Cura.
End G-code END_PRINT It calls the END_PRINT macro from macros.cfg.
Conclusion If you followed the steps, make sure you calibrated your z_offset and your bed mesh. Then you are ready to print your first object with Klipper.
If you also would like to re-enable the stock filament runout sensor, there is a separate post about that: Re-enable the Filament Runout Sensor of the Artillery Sidewinder X2
Further links For further steps and more details, it is always a very good idea to walk through the official documentation:
Klipper documentation Mainsail documentation Moonraker documentation Please leave a comment if something is wrong or missing, or if you have any questions. Have fun!

The Sidewinder X2 comes with the Marlin 2.x firmware, installed on its “Artillery_Ruby” mainboard. This article shows you one easy way to replace Marlin with Klipper as an alternative firmware on your Sidewinder X2.
Be aware that the installed touch display, the USB port, and the SD card slot are unusable with Klipper, because the way they work and are connected is not compatible with it. On my printer, I decided to disconnect them and replace them with dummy prints, but you don’t have to.
Caution: Do this only if you feel experienced enough. You do it at your own risk, and you will probably lose the Artillery warranty. I am not responsible for damages of any kind.
Update (November 2026): My Sidewinder X2 printer.cfg is part of the official Klipper examples now, the supported Raspberry Pi models and the MainsailOS login changed, and the MainsailOS and Mainsail links point to the current documentation.
Requirements An Artillery Sidewinder X2 with unmodified hardware and an Artillery Ruby V1.2 mainboard A Raspberry Pi (Zero 2, 3, or 4; a Pi 5 is supported, too) or a similar compatible board with SD card, power supply, and USB connection to your printer A working PC to flash the Pi and to use as a remote SSH console The will to open your printer (and the potential loss of warranty) Some experience with Linux and the bash console Install MainsailOS Flash an SD card for your Raspberry Pi with MainsailOS. It’s a prepared Raspberry Pi OS Lite with a modern software stack to control your printer. The frontend in this case is Mainsail by default. It’s similar to OctoPrint, but more modern and made for Klipper driven printers only. Follow the official MainsailOS installation guide for the Raspberry Pi. It uses the Raspberry Pi Imager, where you can also set hostname, user, password, Wi-Fi, and SSH before writing the card. There is also a simple article on All3DP. Klipper needs a printer.cfg that tells it all about your connected printer hardware. In Marlin, this configuration lives in Configuration.h and Configuration_adv.h and has to be recompiled on every change. In Klipper, it is just a config file, so you don’t have to recompile the whole firmware on changes. There are a lot of example configs in the Klipper repository. For the Sidewinder X2, I created one: printer-artillery-sidewinder-x2-2022.cfg. My Klipper pull request got merged into the official Klipper examples in October 2022, so you find it there. Copy its content into your printer.cfg. MainsailOS ships a mainsail.cfg with everything Mainsail needs on the Klipper side. Add [include mainsail.cfg] to your printer.cfg. The documentation page mainsail.cfg explains what it provides. Flash Klipper to the printer mainboard As mentioned in the caution above, be sure you know what you are doing. I never tried to switch back to Marlin. Normally, it should be no problem, but I have not tried it at the time of writing (comments are welcome).
You have to bridge two pins to enable the “flash mode” of your mainboard. Open your printer (screws on the bottom). Connect the pins BOOT0 and +3.3V with a jumper or a breadboard cable. (You have to remove it after flashing!)
Connect your Raspberry Pi to your Artillery Sidewinder X2 with a USB cable. Then power on your printer and your Raspberry Pi. Connect to the Pi using SSH, or connect a keyboard and monitor to it. Log in with the user and password you set in the Raspberry Pi Imager. The MainsailOS documentation names pi and raspberry as the defaults, but recommends changing the password.
Before flashing, you have to configure and build the firmware for your printer once. Open the console of your Pi and type
cd ~/klipper/ make menuconfig In the configuration menu, change only the following:
Set Micro-controller Architecture to STMicroelectronics STM32 Set Processor model to STM32F401 Set Bootloader offset to No bootloader Quit (Q) and save (Y) Build the firmware with
make Flash the built firmware with
make flash FLASH_DEVICE=/dev/serial/by-id/usb-Klipper_stm32f401xc_4F006F000351383532393535-if00 In your case, the device may have another ID or path. Adapt the command if so. As mentioned in the caution above, be sure you know what you are doing.
Read more details in the official Klipper documentation: Building and flashing the micro-controller
Remove the flash mode jumper you set above.
Check and calibrate your setup Reboot your Raspberry Pi and follow the Mainsail and Klipper configuration checks.
Follow the Klipper config checks. Ignore OctoPrint, because your setup uses Mainsail instead. Make sure some values are adapted and calibrated for your individual printer: Especially the z-offset And the extruder rotation_distance (Measure it without an installed nozzle!) Calibrate the PID values for the heat bed and the extruder nozzle. Don’t forget to set up or adapt the start and end G-code of your slicer. Next steps These follow-up posts build on this setup:
A useful set of G-code macros (filament runout, pause and resume, start and stop print): Must-Have Mainsail, Klipper, and Cura Configuration for the Artillery Sidewinder X2 Re-enabling the stock filament runout sensor: Re-enable the Filament Runout Sensor of the Artillery Sidewinder X2 Installing an ADXL345 acceleration sensor and calibrating Klipper Resonance Compensation: Install the ADXL345 and Calibrate Input Shaping on the Artillery Sidewinder X2 and Genius Pro Removing and replacing the USB port, the SD card slot, and the useless touch display Conclusion You are done and ready to get in touch with Klipper and its endless possibilities. It takes a while to understand the context. I hope I could help you with the painful start and the initial basic configuration of your Artillery Sidewinder X2.

I show you how to flash the latest Marlin firmware to your Artillery Sidewinder X2. I had to compile it myself because Artillery has not updated it yet. At the time of writing, it’s an adapted version of Marlin 2.1.2.
Caution: No warranty, no support. Do it only if you know what you are doing. It’s absolutely your own risk, and I’m not responsible for any problems or defects.
Requirements Software Pronterface/Printrun STM32CubeProgrammer (you have to register to download it) Customized Marlin Artillery Sidewinder X2 Firmware What you get Marlin 2.x, a precompiled version for the Artillery Sidewinder X2 (Artillery Ruby v1.2 mainboard).
It’s for everyone who has the new Artillery Sidewinder X2 with the new TFT (GD32F305). I compiled a minimal customized firmware for the Artillery Ruby mainboard (not for the TFT controller, as there is no known support yet).
Basically, I enabled some features, like Linear Advance or the OctoPrint support (config and plugin suggestions). I didn’t enable all the features that are relevant for the BigTreeTech TFT firmware, because the custom firmware can’t be flashed on the recently shipped GD32F305 chipset.
I also left unsupported hardware features disabled. For details, see the Configuration.h and Configuration_adv.h.
Flash the firmware Install Pronterface Install STM32CubeProgrammer Power on your Artillery Sidewinder X2 Connect your PC/Mac/laptop with USB to your Sidewinder Start Pronterface Connect to your printer with 115200 baud Type M997 at the bottom right Error messages can be ignored If you are using Windows, look into your device manager to check whether there is a “STM32 Bootloader” Disconnect Pronterface Start STM32CubeProgrammer Connect with USB Make a backup of your original firmware Flash the modified firmware: Download the firmware.bin from the latest release on my GitHub releases page. In STM32CubeProgrammer, open the file, select the firmware, and press Download Disconnect the USB cable from your printer and restart it (power off, then on) Reset the EEPROM with M502 and save the EEPROM settings with the M500 command Set up the basic parameters after the reset You reset your EEPROM (your printer configuration) to the firmware defaults. You should at least set up some basic parameters before you print your next wonderful thing.
Your Z-probe offset (first layer, babysteps) with M851 Z-[your new value] Your extruder E-steps with M92 E[your new value] Your auto bed leveling: home with G28, probe with G29, and enable it afterwards with M420 S1 Don’t forget to save your settings into your EEPROM again with M500.
Conclusion You’re done. I hope I could help.
Special thanks to PrEzi, whose guide helped me to understand this, and of course to all the people he already mentioned.

I bought my first 3D printer. Yes, I finally did it. After reading blogs and ratings and watching some YouTube videos, I chose an Artillery Sidewinder X2. This article tells you why I think it was a good decision.
Pros and cons At the time of writing, the Artillery Sidewinder X2 is a really smart choice if you don’t want to spend an exorbitant amount of money. You get features like a 300x300x400 mm printable volume, a direct extruder, auto bed leveling, an included color touch display, and a filament sensor. On top of that, it’s a really silent printer. The heat bed not only heats up ultra fast, its 220/110V voltage also needs no big power supply, so the installed power supply needs only a semi-passive silent fan.
On the downside, this heat bed is a bit problematic in reality, because its construction has a very uneven temperature distribution. I think you just have to be aware of that fact and adjust the temperature if needed.
Also, if you read through some other blogs and YouTube channels, some people complain about the BLTouch auto bed leveling sensor clone installed on the Sidewinder. I personally can’t complain about it, but I have to say that I haven’t worked with an original BLTouch sensor yet.
Positive Negative Medium printing volume (300x300x400 mm) Direct extruder Auto bed leveling No original BLTouch, an Artillery clone with good precision Color touch display Ultra fast 220/110V coated glass heat bed Uneven heat bed temperature distribution Silent printing, drives, power supply Conclusion That’s a great package for this money from Artillery. See my other posts for how to update to the latest Marlin firmware and, for more advanced makers, how to use Klipper with your Artillery Sidewinder X2.

Are you one of the nerds who like to develop your own game, fancy graphics, or any aspect that comes with that? Or would you like to take your first steps with the young programming language Rust, which unites the speed of C/C++ with memory and thread safety?
Why not combine both to have some fun learning new things?
Just to be even more nerdy, I show you a way to do all of that within the Windows Subsystem for Linux and its graphical extension (WSLg) under Windows 11. When I wrote this post, WSLg was still a preview with some shortcomings.
Update (November 2026): The Rust setup now uses rust-analyzer instead of the deprecated RLS, the fish PATH step is simplified, the Bevy dependency list follows the current Bevy documentation, and the WSLg remarks reflect that it is now part of regular WSL.
Requirements Microsoft Windows 11 CPU virtualization enabled Install WSL2 If you haven’t installed WSL2 yet, follow the official WSL installation guide.
In short:
Open a Windows terminal with administrator privileges (Windows Terminal on GitHub).
Run
wsl --install and follow the instructions.
Configure Linux in WSL2 Open your Ubuntu Linux within WSL2.
Install Rust with
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh rustup update rustup component add rust-analyzer rust-src Remarks: RLS is deprecated and replaced by rust-analyzer, which is why the command installs rust-analyzer instead of rls and rust-analysis. With the original post’s Ubuntu 20.04, the packages from the repository were missing libraries for code completion in VS Code. I have not re-checked that with a current Ubuntu.
If you are using the fish shell:
The rustup installer sets up fish itself if fish is installed when you run it: it creates ~/.config/fish/conf.d/rustup.fish, which sources env.fish. If cargo is not found in fish anyway, create or edit the file ~/.config/fish/conf.d/myconfig.fish.
Add
fish_add_path ~/.cargo/bin Install the Bevy Linux dependencies with
sudo apt install g++ pkg-config libx11-dev libasound2-dev libudev-dev libxkbcommon-x11-0 libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev mesa-vulkan-drivers The libwayland-dev and libxkbcommon-dev packages are only optional if you disable Bevy’s wayland feature, and mesa-vulkan-drivers is one of several Vulkan driver options depending on your graphics card. You can find more information in the Bevy Linux dependencies documentation.
Install git
sudo apt install git Try Bevy Bevy is a slim and fast Rust game engine.
Clone the Bevy repo:
git clone https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy Try the examples in the examples folder:
cargo run --example breakout WSLg is no longer a preview: Linux GUI apps are now officially supported on WSL2. To get hardware accelerated OpenGL rendering through a virtual GPU, install the matching Intel, AMD, or NVIDIA vGPU driver described in the guide to Linux GUI apps on WSL.
Conclusion This is a very good starting point to learn Rust by playing around with a game engine. Let me know about your progress with it.

This week, Microsoft released its first native package manager for Windows 10. If you have ever worked with a package manager for Linux (e.g. apt, pacman), you know the benefits. Or, if you are a developer, you have surely heard of nuget, maven, npm, or similar. It makes it easy to install, uninstall, or update one or all of the applications on your system.
Now you will say that’s old hat, because Chocolatey already exists. You are right, and at the moment it’s even more advanced.
Anyway, WinGet is officially supported and developed under the guidance of Microsoft, and it is now part of Windows itself. So for me, that’s the way to go.
Update (November 2026): WinGet is now included in Windows 11 and current Windows 10 as part of the App Installer, so the preview-period instructions for installing it manually are mostly obsolete. The requirements and the install sections are updated accordingly.
Requirements The client requires Windows 10 1809 (build 17763), Windows 11, Windows Server 2025, or later.
Install WinGet Automatically with the Microsoft Store The client is distributed within the App Installer package. On Windows 11 and current Windows 10, App Installer is a system component that is delivered and updated by the Microsoft Store, so WinGet is usually already there. If winget is not found right after your first login, give Windows a moment to register it, or install or update App Installer from the Microsoft Store.
Manually If the Store is not available (e.g. in a sandbox), you can install it manually. You get the same package from the WinGet releases page. Download and execute the Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller_8wekyb3d8bbwe.msixbundle. Note that this package does not update itself via the Microsoft Store. See the official Readme.md for more information.
Configure WinGet After the installation, open the Windows command line (cmd.exe) or a PowerShell.
If you start it as an administrator, you don’t have to accept the elevation dialogs later on.
Before you install your applications, I recommend modifying some settings first. Customize some basic settings before you install or upgrade applications with WinGet for the first time.
Edit the settings file by executing
winget settings In the opened settings.json file, set up your preferred language priority list (e.g. to German) and set your installation scope to machine (instead of user local).
{ "installBehavior": { "preferences": { "locale": ["de-DE", "en-US"], "scope": "machine" } } } A complete list of settings can be found in the WinGet settings documentation.
Use WinGet As an example, let us search for PeaZip, a nice open-source compression and decompression application that supports most of the compression algorithms out there.
Just run the following command.
winget search PeaZip If you are unsure whether the result is the application you searched for, you can run the winget show command with one of the found application IDs.
winget show Giorgiotani.Peazip You should get more information about the package to be installed.
If you got the right package, install the found Giorgiotani.Peazip package.
winget install PeaZip -h The parameter -h hides the installer assistant and just installs the application silently to the program files folder. If you used the scope local in the settings preferences above, the installed application is placed in your user account’s AppData folder.
To upgrade an installed application to the latest version, run the upgrade option. As always, if you are unsure about the application name, use its ID instead.
winget upgrade PeaZip -h And finally, one of my favorites. Like the Linux command apt-get upgrade, you can just run
winget upgrade --all -h to update all installed applications that can be found in the repository to their latest version. Because we also set the -h parameter, it’s done silently again.
Conclusion Here it is, a native package manager for Windows applications. Yes, it’s version 1.0, and you can’t expect to find your lovely package every time or to get a fancy UI. But for the applications it finds, the repeated sessions of searching, downloading, and updating are gone. Just run an upgrade --all from time to time (or automate it) and you are done.
This tool saves you a lot of time.

I will start a series of posts about configuring Arch Linux in a slim, straightforward way. But let me begin with some pros and cons of the Arch Linux distribution.
Update (November 2026): I originally claimed that both Slackware and Gentoo are rolling releases like Arch Linux. That is only true for Gentoo; Slackware uses stable releases, and the section below is corrected.
The Arch Linux distribution describes itself as “a lightweight and flexible Linux distribution that tries to Keep It Simple”.
That’s it: Arch Linux is absolutely the right distribution for you if you like a system that only does what you have installed and configured. It does it only that way, and no magic happens. In addition, it has a great community with an up-to-date wiki about nearly all aspects of the system. So if you have to configure a package, it’s mostly enough to follow the associated article there.
Widely used distributions There is no need to dive in as deeply as you have to with Slackware or Gentoo. For example, normally you don’t have to compile anything, but you have the freedom to do it anyway. Like Arch Linux, Gentoo is a rolling release. Slackware is not: it has stable point releases (version 15.0 came out in February 2022), plus a -current development branch that is not meant for production systems. With a rolling release, you can always have the latest stable version of the kernel and all software packages, mostly on the same day of their release. That’s a big pro for update junkies, and you never have to do a big upgrade after half a year of waiting.
On the other hand, there are Debian-based distributions like Ubuntu. They work out of the box. They have a graphical installer, pre-configured packages, and proprietary drivers for, e.g., graphics cards. Most Debian-based distributions are not rolling releases. They have big releases from time to time, and you can choose to upgrade or stay with your release for a while. Updates are mostly security fixes only. If you are a beginner or just want a good-looking Linux without having to worry about internals, choose one of them.
Conclusion In my opinion, Arch Linux hits the sweet spot. Without spending most of your time configuring details, you get an always up-to-date, slim distribution. And while working with it, you have the chance to learn a lot about how the Linux ecosystem works.
In future posts, I will help you with some aspects of it.
